system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 15 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2171-02-23 00:04:00 to 2171-03-09 14:25:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman was admitted for worsening lower extremity edema in the setting of chronic lymphedema, morbid obesity, and recurrent cellulitis. She presented with increased swelling up to her thighs, shortness of breath on exertion, and concern for possible cellulitis in the right foot. Initial labs showed leukocytosis and normal BNP, with a clear chest X-ray, ruling out acute heart failure. She was treated with IV furosemide, adjusted for rising creatinine, and a short course of IV clindamycin for possible cellulitis, later discontinued due to lack of improvement. A transient neurologic event was evaluated by neurology and attributed to factors including volume status and sedating medications, with a normal Keppra level. Gabapentin was started for neuropathic pain, and nystatin for oral thrush. She stabilized with improved edema, continued home medications, and was discharged home with home health services and follow-up plans.
problems: Morbid (severe) obesity due to excess calories
Elevated white blood cell count, unspecified
Personal history of other venous thrombosis and embolism
Epilepsy, unspecified, not intractable, without status epilepticus
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of other organs and systems

diagnoses.long_title: Morbid (severe) obesity due to excess calories
Epilepsy, unspecified, not intractable, without status epilepticus
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of other organs and systems
Personal history of other venous thrombosis and embolism

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in tonight for worsening leg swelling and redness. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my legs have been swelling more over the past week. They’re red and warm, especially on the lower parts. My primary doctor saw me yesterday and said it might be cellulitis, so he started me on IV antibiotics through my PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how’s the redness been since starting the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s a little better, but now two of my toes are getting redder. I’m also feeling short of breath when I walk, and I’ve had some wheezing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. We’ll monitor that. Your vitals are stable, and your chest X-ray came back clear, so it doesn’t look like heart failure is the main issue. We’ll continue the IV clindamycin for the infection and start IV furosemide to help with the swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on bumetanide at home—4 mg daily. I was on every other day for a bit, but when the swelling came back, I went back to daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll use stronger IV diuretics here to help get the fluid off faster. We also noticed your INR was high when we checked—likely because of the antibiotics affecting your warfarin. We’ll hold the warfarin for now and start a heparin drip to keep your blood thinning safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I didn’t know antibiotics could do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, some can. We’ll watch it closely and restart your warfarin when it’s safe. For now, focus on resting and letting the treatment work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The swelling hasn’t gone down much, but my breathing feels a bit easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your white blood cell count is elevated, which supports the infection. But your kidney function is a little worse—creatinine went up from 1.2 to 1.4. So we’re adjusting your diuretic to avoid stressing your kidneys too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mild and expected with aggressive diuresis. We’re monitoring it closely. We’ve switched from IV furosemide twice daily to a continuous drip to be gentler on your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your redness is improving, which is a good sign the antibiotics are working. You’re on day two of IV clindamycin, and we’ll continue for a full 10-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my weight? I think I gained about 9 pounds before coming in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You weighed 352.7 pounds on admission. We’re tracking daily weights. So far, you’ve lost about 2 pounds, which is slow but expected given how hard it is to remove fluid in lymphedema.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s frustrating. I eat low salt and take my meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Lymphedema makes fluid control very tough. We’ll keep working on it. Also, we noticed you have oral thrush—white patches in your mouth. Were you on nystatin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to fluconazole, an oral antifungal. It works better for thrush and should clear it up in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is coming down. It was 4.2 on admission, now it’s 2.8. We’re restarting your warfarin at 7 mg daily and will keep checking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your history of DVT and PE, we have to be careful. The ultrasound showed no new clots, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is stable, and you’re using your inhalers as needed. The wheezing is mild. We’ll keep monitoring your COPD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t needed them much today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Also, we’re continuing your high-dose pain meds for fibromyalgia, but the team noted you’ve been very sleepy. We’ll discuss this with your PCP after discharge to see if adjustments are needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I’m on a lot, but the pain is real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe you. It’s just about balancing pain control with safety. We’ll make sure your PCP has all the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your redness is much better, and the new redness in your toes hasn’t spread. That’s a good sign the infection is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. My legs still hurt, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain is likely from the swelling and skin changes. We’ll keep managing it with your current meds and compression as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your weight is now 160.4 kg—down about 1 kg from admission. It’s slow, but we’re making progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Only a kilo? I feel like I should be losing more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With severe lymphedema and obesity, fluid is very hard to remove. We’ve had to slow down the diuretics to protect your kidneys. It’s a balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess I’ll have to be patient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your thrush is improving. You’re on day four of fluconazole—just a few more doses to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth feels better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re also keeping you on the nicotine patch since you’re not smoking in the hospital. Your PCP can help with long-term cessation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like to quit, honestly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great goal. We’ll make a note to discuss support options at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now stable at 2.5. You’re back on your regular warfarin dose and no longer need the heparin drip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was nervous about being on the drip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. Now it’s back to your usual routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re wrapping up your IV antibiotics today—final dose of clindamycin. The cellulitis has resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll keep you on your home diuretic, bumetanide 4 mg daily, and monitor your fluid balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your weight has stabilized around 159 kg. We’ve stopped the IV diuretics and you’re doing well on oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel lighter, at least.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared for discharge tomorrow. We’ll send you home with instructions to finish the fluconazole and continue all your regular medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? I thought I’d be here longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made good progress. Infection is gone, breathing is stable, and your labs are acceptable. You’ll follow up with your PCP in a week for labs and warfarin checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your PCP wants to keep it for now, but we recommend reevaluating it soon. Long-term PICCs can lead to complications like clots or infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final day! Your discharge papers are ready. You’ll go home with home health services to help with monitoring and care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep taking your meds, watch for any redness or swelling, and call your doctor if anything changes. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember to take your fluconazole until it’s gone, and get your labs done in a week. Call if you have fever, increased swelling, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. You’ve done well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in with your discharge paperwork and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your friend is listed as your contact. Make sure she knows to call if you’re not feeling well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’s picking me up and will check on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Stay safe and take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Have a good trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch with your PCP to coordinate follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Feel free to call the office if you have questions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Get some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman was admitted for worsening bilateral lower extremity edema and cellulitis, with a history of chronic lymphedema, morbid obesity, and recurrent infections. She presented with increased swelling, erythema, and mild shortness of breath, and was found to have leukocytosis and stable renal function. Treatment included a 10-day course of IV clindamycin for cellulitis, IV diuresis with furosemide that was later transitioned to oral bumetanide, and management of a supratherapeutic INR due to antibiotic interaction by temporarily holding warfarin and initiating a heparin drip. Her infection resolved, INR stabilized, and she was discharged home on her baseline medications, including warfarin and bumetanide, with instructions to complete a course of fluconazole for oral thrush and follow up for lab monitoring. Despite aggressive diuresis, weight reduction was minimal due to the challenges of fluid management in severe lymphedema.
